claims.claim_text: The location has been identified by Christian tradition as the birthplace of Jesus since the 2nd century.
A church was first completed there in AD 339; the replacement building after a 6th-century fire retains mosaics from the original.
Battir is a Palestinian cultural landscape of dry-stone terraces and a complex irrigation system supporting olives and vegetables.
The family water-distribution system uses a time-managed rotation and mathematical allocation.
The old town substantially preserves Mamluk urban morphology with later Ottoman additions.
The Al-Ibrahimi Mosque/Tomb of Patriarchs monumental compound is central to the old town and the enclosure dates to the 1st century AD.
The place is venerated by Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
The monumental enclosure around the sacred cave was constructed in the 1st century AD.
The site is associated with traditions concerning Abraham/Ibrahim and is venerated by three monotheistic religions.

The property contains deposits of human activity dating to about 10,500 BC.
By the 9th–8th millennium BC it was a sizeable permanent settlement with surviving wall, ditch and tower.
Middle Bronze Age remains indicate a large Canaanite city-state.
The State of Palestine submitted Sebastia to UNESCO's Tentative List in 2012.
The submission describes it as the Iron Age II capital and a major Hellenistic/Roman urban centre, and records major excavation campaigns.
Christian and Islamic traditions associate the site with John the Baptist/Yahya.
The State Party submission dates the complex to 724–743 AD and says it was most likely built by Hisham and later decorated by al-Walid II.
The submission records destruction in the 749 earthquake and excavations from 1935–1948 by the Palestinian Department of Antiquities under Dimitri Baramki with Robert Hamilton.
The site includes a major bath complex and extensive mosaic decoration, including the Tree of Life panel.
Silwan is part of the geo-historic context immediately outside the Old City; the Gihon Spring is identified in a State Party submission as a focal water source in Jerusalem's development.
UNESCO monitoring documents record reports and concerns concerning excavation and tunnelling activities in Silwan.
Canaanite/Roman/Islamic period sequence for the whole town
Specific excavation impacts and current physical condition
The Western/Wailing Wall is identified by UNESCO as one of the major monuments of the Old City property.
A 1930 international commission was established to determine Muslim and Jewish rights and claims connected with the Wall.
Suq al-Qattanin is a Mamluk market terminating at Tariq al-Wad and connecting through Bab al-Qattanin to the Haram al-Sharif precinct.
Exact patron and construction date pending direct bibliography inspection
The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate maintains the living tradition identifying the Gethsemane shrine as the Tomb of the Virgin Mary.
The Studium Biblicum Franciscanum records archaeological excavation work at Gethsemane and the Tomb of Mary.
Al-Wad Street contains major Mamluk architectural institutions and connects with the Qattanin market/gate complex.
Individual dates, patrons, coordinates, and rights
The present citadel is a multi-period composition incorporating Roman fortification and Crusader, Ayyubid, Mamluk, and Ottoman construction.
Exact attribution of each tower and phase
The Church of the Holy Sepulchre is a major monument within the Old City World Heritage property; UNESCO identifies the Resurrection rotunda as housing Christ's tomb within Christian tradition.
The Studium Biblicum Franciscanum records archaeological excavation work at the Holy Sepulchre.

A UNESCO monitoring document records the Jordanian and Palestinian report describing Nabi Dawoud Mosque as an Islamic Waqf property next to the southern wall of the Old City and reporting alterations there.
Mount Zion forms part of the wider geo-historic and religious context described in a postponed State Party extension proposal.
Tell Rumeida is included in the archaeological remains of the buffer-zone context of Hebron/Al-Khalil Old Town.
ICOMOS documented that Tell Rumeida was excluded from the original nominated property boundary and discussed evidence of earlier settlement in its vicinity.
The Nabi Yunus mosque/maqam is in old Halhul; the monument record dates it to AH 623 / AD 1226, identifies an Ayyubid patron, and records later Mamluk renovation.
WAFA documents the existence of Nabi Nuh shrine in Dura as a local religious and historical landmark and records community restoration and charitable use by 2020.
UNESCO identifies the sacred Cave of Machpelah/al-Ghar al-Sharif inside the monumental Al-Ibrahimi Mosque/Tomb of Patriarchs complex and treats its burial associations as tradition.
ICOMOS specifically discusses the Sheikh Ali al-Bakka area as an excluded area relevant to the integrity and earlier street patterns of Hebron Old Town.
The conservation project documents three historic pools and an Ottoman Murad castle; the project was completed in 2012 using distinguishable and reversible interventions.
The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate officially lists a Monastery of St George in Al-Khader.
Synonymy of Deir al-Jannah and St George monastery
The Patriarchate's institutional history places the formation of Saint Savvas' Lavra around AD 483 and describes long continuous monastic activity.
A substantial published excavation corpus exists for Herodium, including Corbo's palace-fortress report and later final reports for the 1972–2010 excavations.
Published academic chapters address Byzantine churches and inscriptions at Herodion.
The conservation record identifies an Ottoman Murad castle as part of the Solomon's Pools historical-site complex.
The Milk Grotto is a local sanctuary near the Nativity Basilica with a living devotion shared by Christian and Muslim women.
The SBF records an emergency excavation at the sanctuary in October 2005.
UNESCO lists the Great Omari Mosque among the cultural properties in Gaza with verified damage.
The 2026 State of Palestine Tentative List submission identifies it as the central congregational mosque of historic Gaza and describes Mamluk and Ottoman enlargement of a layered monument.
Exact destruction severity and surviving fabric
UNESCO lists Tell el-Ajjul among the archaeological sites with verified damage.
Academic and museum records identify Tell el-Ajjul as a separate Bronze Age archaeological site south of modern Gaza City, with excavated Middle and Late Bronze Age material.
Exact urban identification with ancient Gaza
Current damage severity and site boundary
UNESCO lists Hamam As-Samra among Gaza properties with verified damage.
A Palestinian cultural-sector report hosted by UNESCO reported complete destruction on 30 December 2023 and described the bath as Gaza's last surviving historic hammam.
UNESCO lists Qal'at Barqouq in Khan Younis among properties with verified damage.
The hosted Palestinian report attributes the castle to 1387 in the reign of Sultan Barquq and describes a caravan-route function and surviving façade.
UNESCO lists the Saint Porphyrios Orthodox Church Complex among the Gaza properties with verified damage.

The 2026 State Party submission describes an early fifth-century church that remains an active sanctuary, while the Jerusalem Patriarchate confirms the living ecclesiastical identity of the Gaza monastery.
Exact damage severity and casualty history
The State of Palestine submitted the Historic Centre of Gaza to UNESCO's Tentative List on 13 January 2026, defining a 1.7 km² historic core with four traditional quarters.
UNESCO's March 2026 assessment verifies damage to a large number of named religious, archaeological, civic, and residential heritage properties within Gaza Governorate.
Current integrity of the 1.7 km² property
UNESCO lists Anthedon Harbour among the Gaza sites with verified damage.
The State Party Tentative List describes Anthedon as an ancient seaport in northwest Gaza with multi-period remains and explicitly notes uncertainty in precise site identification.
UNESCO verifies damage to Qal'at Barqouq in Khan Younis Governorate.
A Palestinian report hosted by UNESCO records damage to historic houses in Khan Younis and describes Qal'at Barqouq as a principal historic component.
Current integrity of Khan Younis historic core
UNESCO verifies damage to Tell Rafah in Rafah Governorate.
Exact Tell Rafah chronology and boundary
Current damage severity beyond UNESCO's verification
Old Nablus is a historic urban cluster with Roman, Islamic, medieval, Ottoman, religious, commercial, residential, and water-related components.
UNESCO and partners completed restoration and adaptive reuse of Khan al-Wakala as a component of Old Nablus.
Al-Nasr Mosque is an identified spatial component bordering Bab al-Saha and Al-Nasr Street within Old Nablus.
Mount Gerizim is the living sacred centre of the Samaritan community and contains major Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, and Islamic remains.
Al-Yasmina is one of the recognized quarters of Old Nablus; Hosh al-Atout preserves Ottoman residential courtyard fabric.
The official portal reports severe damage in 2002 and reconstruction completed in 2012 for Hosh al-Atout.
Khan al-Tujjar is a recognized historic market/fabric-market component of Old Nablus.
Maqam Yusuf near Balata has been revered in Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Samaritan traditions and has had changing Palestinian social and religious meanings.
The inspected academic article states that archaeological evidence does not verify competing burial identifications.
Al-Sibat market is a late Ottoman component within Jenin's older neighbourhoods and is reported above Roman and Byzantine archaeological context.
Fatima Khatun Mosque is a major sixteenth-century Ottoman urban component in central Jenin.
The official Palestinian heritage portal locates Al-Kayed Palace in Sebastia, Nablus Governorate, and dates construction to 1858.
Whether a separate Jenin palace with the same name exists
Burqin Church is a living Greek Orthodox church in Burqin with an official Byzantine heritage attribution.
Tulkarm contains officially recognized built heritage assets, including a museum in a 1908 Ottoman-era building and rehabilitated heritage facilities.
Deir Istiya is a recognized Palestinian historic centre with approximately three-century-old buildings, narrow streets, palaces, springs, caves, and ruins.
The official Deir Istiya record confirms numerous water springs and the nearby perennial Wadi Qana setting.
The official portal documents Ayyubid and Ottoman shrines in Kifl Haris, including inscription-bearing structures.
Tell el-Far'ah North has a major excavation and publication corpus associated with the École biblique and nine campaigns led by Roland de Vaux.
Academic synthesis identifies ordered and fortified Early Bronze settlement phases at Tell el-Far'ah North.
Birzeit contains a governed historic centre whose buildings, public spaces, infrastructure, and boundaries were documented and rehabilitated through a long-term Riwaq programme.
The Palestinian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities provides contextual reference to a fortified castle in Birzeit.
Exact castle identity, date, and surviving fabric
Aboud is recognized within Riwaq's historic-centres programme.
The Aboud landscape includes a sixth-century St Barbara church ruin, a Roman-road and cemetery context, and a separately documented multi-phase Dormition church.
Current condition and rights for each component
Riwaq recognizes Deir Ammar as a Palestinian historic-centre record.
Academic records document Intermediate/Middle Bronze Age shaft-tomb and assemblage evidence at Ain Samiya.
The official Palestinian route guide distinguishes Ain Samiya, Khirbet Marjameh, a palace feature, and Khirbet Samiya within the wider landscape.
Exact relation between cemetery and nearby settlement
Riwaq records conservation and adaptive reuse of the An Nabi Salih Cultural Center complex completed in 2003 with a local partner.
The official Palestinian portal documents monastic caves, a sixth-century monastery phase, and restoration in 1892 at Deir Quruntal.
Ain es-Sultan is the perennial spring adjacent to and included among the attributes of the inscribed Ancient Jericho/Tell es-Sultan property.
Independent site boundary outside the property
The official Palestinian record describes one Nabi Musa shrine complex containing a mosque, mausoleum/tomb, courtyard, rooms, and related facilities.
The wider El-Bariyah landscape contains permanent springs, wadis, monasteries, shrines, and long-term human adaptation to desert water resources.
The official Palestinian portal identifies Nabi Musa as a Mamluk shrine complex associated institutionally with Sultan al-Zahir Baybars.
The State of Palestine's El-Bariyah submission places Maqam an-Nabi Musa within the Islamic sacred and pilgrimage landscape.
